summary.text: Quadratic reciprocity makes \(5\) a square modulo \(p\); choosing an even root \(e\) and setting \(n=e-1\) gives (apart from the direct case \(p=11\)) an odd \(4\le n<p\) with \(p\mid(n^2+2n-4)\). Expressing the continued fraction as a ratio of consecutive terms of an integer recurrence, a Casoratian identity involving \(2(n-1)!\), together with prime-power exponent bounds, shows that every factor of the cofactor \((n^2+2n-4)/p\) cancels from the ratio while \(p\) cannot cancel, leaving exactly \(p\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 R_{n-1}(n)=(n-1)+\frac n4,
 \qquad
 R_k(n)=k-\frac{k+1}{R_{k+1}(n)}\quad(2\le k<n-1).
\]
Thus the continued fraction in the definition of the sequence is \(1/R_2(n)\). If \(R_2(n)=N/D\) in lowest terms, then \(1/R_2(n)=D/N\), so the sequence value \(a(n)\) is \(|N|\). We prove that every prime \(p\equiv1\) or \(9\pmod {10}\) occurs as such a value.

## 1. Integer sequences underlying the continued fraction

Fix \(n\ge 3\). Define integers \(P_k\), for \(2\le k\le n\), downward by
\[
 P_n=4,\qquad P_{n-1}=5n-4,
\]
and
\[
 P_k=kP_{k+1}-(k+1)P_{k+2}\qquad(2\le k\le n-2).
\tag{1}
\]
The endpoint ratio is
\[
 \frac{P_{n-1}}{P_n}=\frac{5n-4}{4}=(n-1)+\frac n4=R_{n-1}(n).
\]
Once it is known that the relevant \(P_j\)'s are nonzero, downward induction using (1) gives
\[
 R_k(n)=\frac{P_k}{P_{k+1}}.
\tag{2}
\]
Indeed, if \(R_{k+1}=P_{k+1}/P_{k+2}\), then
\[
 R_k=k-(k+1)\frac{P_{k+2}}{P_{k+1}}
     =\frac{kP_{k+1}-(k+1)P_{k+2}}{P_{k+1}}
     =\frac{P_k}{P_{k+1}}.
\]

For completeness, the required positivity follows from a simple downward invariant. For \(3\le k\le n-2\), one has
\[
 0<P_{k+1},\qquad
 (k-2)P_{k+1}<P_k<kP_{k+1}.
\tag{3}
\]
At \(k=n-2\), substitute \(P_n=4\), \(P_{n-1}=5n-4\), and
\[
 P_{n-2}=(n-2)(5n-4)-4(n-1).
\]
The upper inequality in (3) follows by subtracting the positive number \(4(n-1)\), while the difference between \(P_{n-2}\) and \((n-4)P_{n-1}\) is
\[
 2(5n-4)-4(n-1)=6n-4>0.
\]
Also \(P_{n-1}>0\). For the induction step, suppose the corresponding bounds at \(k+1\) are known. Thus
\[
 0<P_{k+2},\qquad
 (k-1)P_{k+2}<P_{k+1}<(k+1)P_{k+2}.
\]
Equation (1) immediately gives \(P_k<kP_{k+1}\). Moreover,
\[
 P_k-(k-2)P_{k+1}=2P_{k+1}-(k+1)P_{k+2}>0,
\]
because \(P_{k+1}>(k-1)P_{k+2}\) and \(2(k-1)\ge k+1\) for \(k\ge3\). This proves (3), and in particular every \(P_k\) with \(3\le k\le n\) is positive. The value of \(P_2\), obtained below, is positive as well for \(n\ge4\). Thus (2) is valid.

We next obtain an explicit formula for \(P_2\) and a second identity needed later. Introduce a companion solution \(T_k\) of the same recurrence,
\[
 T_n=0,\qquad T_{n-1}=1,
 \qquad T_k=kT_{k+1}-(k+1)T_{k+2}.
\tag{4}
\]
Also put
\[
 F_k=\prod_{i=k}^{n-1}i,
 \qquad
 \Psi_k=(2-k)F_k,
\]
where an empty product is \(1\). Since \(F_k=kF_{k+1}\), direct substitution shows that \(\Psi_k\) also satisfies recurrence (1). Notice the special values
\[
 \Psi_2=0,
 \qquad \Psi_3=-F_3,
 \qquad \Psi_n=2-n,
 \qquad \Psi_{n-1}=(3-n)(n-1).
\tag{5}
\]

For any two solutions \(X,Y\) of (1), define their discrete Wronskian, or Casoratian, by
\[
 C_k=X_kY_{k+1}-X_{k+1}Y_k.
\]
Using the recurrence for both \(X\) and \(Y\), expansion gives
\[
 C_k=(k+1)C_{k+1}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 C_2=\left(\prod_{i=3}^{n-1}i\right)C_{n-1}=F_3C_{n-1}.
\tag{6}
\]

Apply (6) first to \(T\) and \(\Psi\). By (5), its left side is \(-T_2F_3\), whereas
\[
 C_{n-1}=T_{n-1}\Psi_n-T_n\Psi_{n-1}=2-n.
\]
As \(F_3>0\), cancellation gives
\[
 T_2=n-2.
\tag{7}
\]

Apply (6) next to \(P\) and \(\Psi\). The left side is \(-P_2F_3\), and the endpoint value is
\[
 (5n-4)(2-n)-4(3-n)(n-1)=-(n^2+2n-4).
\]
Cancelling \(F_3\) yields the fundamental formula
\[
 P_2=n^2+2n-4=(n+1)^2-5.
\tag{8}
\]
In particular, \(P_2>0\) for \(n\ge4\).

Finally apply (6) to \(P\) and \(T\). At the upper endpoint,
\[
 C_{n-1}=P_{n-1}T_n-P_nT_{n-1}=-4.
\]
At the lower endpoint, using (7),
\[
 C_2=P_2T_3-(n-2)P_3.
\]
Therefore
\[
 (n-2)P_3=P_2T_3+4F_3.
\tag{9}
\]
Since
\[
 (n-1)!=1\cdot2\cdot3\cdots(n-1)=2F_3,
\]
we may also write
\[
 4F_3=2(n-1)!.
\tag{10}
\]

## 2. A large prime dividing \(P_2\) cannot divide \(P_3\)

We record a fact that will ensure that the desired prime remains in the reduced numerator of \(P_2/P_3\).

Suppose that \(p\) is prime, \(p>n\ge4\), and \(p\mid P_2\). Then
\[
 p\nmid P_3.
\tag{11}
\]
For if \(p\) divided both \(P_2\) and \(P_3\), recurrence (1) would propagate this divisibility upward. More explicitly, if \(p\mid P_j,P_{j+1}\), then (1) rearranges to
\[
 (j+1)P_{j+2}=jP_{j+1}-P_j.
\]
Hence \(p\mid(j+1)P_{j+2}\). But \(1\le j+1\le n<p\), so the prime \(p\) does not divide \(j+1\), and therefore \(p\mid P_{j+2}\). Beginning with \(j=2\), this proves \(p\mid P_n\). That is impossible because \(P_n=4\) while \(p>n\ge4\). This proves (11).

## 3. Cancellation of every small prime power in \(P_2\)

The main arithmetic step is to show that, apart from a possible prime factor larger than \(n\), the entire prime-power part of \(P_2\) also divides \(P_3\).

We first establish a bound on exponents.

**Exponent bound.** Let \(q\le n\) be an odd prime. If
\[
 q^a\mid P_2,
\]
then
\[
 aq\le n-1.
\tag{12}
\]

Assume for contradiction that \(n-1<aq\). Write
\[
 N=n+1.
\]
By (8),
\[
 P_2=N^2-5.
\tag{13}
\]
We split according to \(a\).

If \(a=0\), then \(n-1<0\), which is impossible.

If \(a=1\), the inequalities \(n-1<q\le n\) imply \(q=n\). Since \(q\mid P_2=n^2+2n-4\), it follows that \(n\mid4\). With \(n\ge4\), this forces \(n=4\), but \(4\) is not prime. This is impossible.

Suppose \(a=2\). Then \(n-1<2q\), so
\[
 q+1\le N\le2q+1.
\tag{14}
\]
Write \(P_2=q^2d\), with \(d\) a positive integer. Equations (13) and (14) give
\[
 N^2=q^2d+5.
\tag{15}
\]
They also force \(d\le4\): if \(d\ge5\), then the right side of (15) is at least \(5q^2+5\), while \(N^2\le(2q+1)^2\), and for \(q\ge3\) one has \(5q^2+5>(2q+1)^2\).

There are now four cases.

* If \(d=1\), then \(N\ge q+1\) gives \(N^2\ge(q+1)^2>q^2+5\), contrary to (15).
* If \(d=2\), then, because \(q\) is odd, \(q^2\equiv1\pmod8\), and (15) says \(N^2\equiv7\pmod8\). But the only square residues modulo \(8\) are \(0,1,4\).
* If \(d=3\), equation (15) says \(N^2\equiv2\pmod3\), impossible because the square residues modulo \(3\) are \(0,1\).
* If \(d=4\), then \(N^2=4q^2+5\). If \(N\le2q\), this is plainly impossible. The only remaining possibility allowed by (14) is \(N=2q+1\), but then comparison gives \(4q^2+4q+1=4q^2+5\), or \(q=1\), again impossible.

Thus \(a=2\) cannot violate (12).

It remains to treat \(a\ge3\). First note three elementary nondivisibility facts following from (8):
\[
 3\nmid P_2,\qquad 7\nmid P_2,\qquad 25\nmid P_2.
\tag{16}
\]
Indeed, \(P_2=(n+1)^2-5\). Modulo \(3\), this would require a square to equal \(2\); modulo \(7\), it would require a square to equal \(5\), whereas the square residues modulo \(7\) are \(0,1,2,4\). Finally, if \(x^2\equiv5\pmod {25}\), reduction modulo \(5\) forces \(5\mid x\), hence \(x^2\equiv0\pmod {25}\), a contradiction. Thus a prime \(q\) occurring to exponent at least \(3\) is neither \(3\), \(5\), nor \(7\). Since it is odd, it follows that
\[
 q\ge11.
\tag{17}
\]

For \(q\ge11\) and \(a\ge3\), one has
\[
 (aq+1)^2<q^a.
\tag{18}
\]
This can be proved by induction on \(a\). The base case is the direct inequality \((3q+1)^2<q^3\) for \(q\ge11\). For the induction step, multiply the inequality for \(a\) by \(q\), and use the elementary estimate
\[
 ((a+1)q+1)^2\le q(aq+1)^2
\]
valid for \(q\ge11\) and \(a\ge3\).

Now the assumed failure of (12) gives \(n\le aq\), hence \(N=n+1\le aq+1\). Since \(q^a\mid P_2\) and \(P_2>0\),
\[
 q^a\le P_2=N^2-5<N^2\le(aq+1)^2,
\]
contradicting (18). This completes the proof of the exponent bound (12).

We now use (12) to prove the promised cancellation statement. Let \(q\le n\) be an odd prime, and let \(a\) be the exact exponent of \(q\) in \(P_2\). Then
\[
 q^a\mid P_3.
\tag{19}
\]
If \(a=0\), this is trivial. Otherwise, (12) gives \(aq\le n-1\). Consequently \(q^a\mid(n-1)!\). One way to see this is to observe that the \(a\) distinct multiples \(q,2q,\ldots,aq\) all occur among the factors of \((n-1)!\), and their product is \(q^a a!\). By (10), it follows that
\[
 q^a\mid4F_3.
\tag{20}
\]
Also, \(q\nmid n-2\). For if \(q\mid n-2\), then because \(a>0\), \(q\mid P_2\), while the identity
\[
 P_2=(n-2)(n+4)+4
\]
would imply \(q\mid4\). An odd prime cannot divide \(4\).

Now (9), together with \(q^a\mid P_2\) and (20), shows that
\[
 q^a\mid(n-2)P_3.
\]
Since \(q\nmid n-2\), the numbers \(q^a\) and \(n-2\) are coprime. Therefore \(q^a\mid P_3\), proving (19).

## 4. Reduction of \(P_2/P_3\) when a large prime divides \(P_2\)

We now prove the key assembly statement. Suppose
\[
 n\ge4,\qquad n\text{ is odd},\qquad p\text{ is prime},\qquad n<p,
 \qquad p\mid P_2.
\tag{21}
\]
Then
\[
 a(n)=p.
\tag{22}
\]

Put
\[
 s=\frac{P_2}{p},
\]
so that \(P_2=ps\). We first show
\[
 s\mid P_3.
\tag{23}
\]
It suffices to check every prime power dividing \(s\).

From (8),
\[
 P_2+5=(n+1)^2,
\]
so
\[
 P_2<(n+1)^2\le p^2.
\tag{24}
\]
Thus \(p\nmid s\), since otherwise \(p^2\mid P_2\), contradicting (24).

The number \(P_2\) is odd. Indeed, \(n\) is odd, so \(n+1\) is even and \((n+1)^2-5\) is odd. Hence no positive power of \(2\) divides \(s\).

Let \(q^k\mid s\), where \(q\ne p\) is an odd prime. Then \(q^k\mid P_2\). If \(q\le n\), statement (19), applied to the full exponent of \(q\) in \(P_2\), shows in particular that \(q^k\mid P_3\).

There cannot be a prime \(q>n\), \(q\ne p\), dividing \(s\). If there were, both \(p\) and \(q\) would divide \(P_2\); as distinct primes they are coprime, so \(pq\mid P_2\). But \(p,q\ge n+1\), whence
\[
 (n+1)^2\le pq\le P_2,
\]
contradicting (24). We have therefore accounted for every prime power dividing \(s\), and (23) follows.

Write
\[
 P_3=sD.
\]
By (11), \(p\nmid P_3\), and hence \(p\nmid D\). Thus \(p\) and \(D\) are coprime. Using (2),
\[
 R_2(n)=\frac{P_2}{P_3}=\frac{sp}{sD}=\frac pD.
\]
Both \(P_3\) and \(s\) are positive, by the positivity established above, so \(D>0\). Since \(\gcd(p,D)=1\), the displayed fraction is in lowest terms and has numerator \(p\). Therefore the reciprocal continued fraction \(1/R_2(n)\) has reduced denominator \(p\). This proves (22).

## 5. Choosing the index by quadratic reciprocity

Let \(p\) now be a prime satisfying
\[
 p\equiv1\quad\text{or}\quad9\pmod {10}.
\tag{25}
\]
Then \(p\ne2,5\), and reducing (25) modulo \(5\) gives
\[
 p\equiv1\quad\text{or}\quad4\pmod5.
\tag{26}
\]
Both \(1\) and \(4\) are nonzero squares modulo \(5\). Since \(5\equiv1\pmod4\), quadratic reciprocity says
\[
 \left(\frac5p\right)=\left(\frac p5\right).
\]
By (26), the right side is \(1\). Hence \(5\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(p\): there is a residue \(y\) such that
\[
 y^2\equiv5\pmod p.
\tag{27}
\]
The residue \(y\) is nonzero, since otherwise \(p\mid5\), contrary to \(p\ne5\).

Choose its representative \(v\) with \(0<v<p\). The two roots \(v\) and \(p-v\) have opposite parity because \(p\) is odd. Select the even one and call it \(e\). Then
\[
 0<e<p,\qquad 2\mid e,\qquad e^2\equiv5\pmod p.
\tag{28}
\]

There is one small exceptional prime, \(p=11\), which we handle directly. For \(n=3\),
\[
 R_2(3)=2+\frac34=\frac{11}{4},
\]
so the continued fraction is \(4/11\), and therefore \(a(3)=11\).

Assume from now on that \(p\ne11\). We claim that the even integer \(e\) in (28) satisfies \(e\ge6\). The only nonnegative even possibilities below \(6\) are \(0,2,4\). Since \(p\mid e^2-5\):

* \(e=0\) would give \(p\mid5\), hence \(p=5\), impossible;
* \(e=2\) would give \(p\mid1\), impossible;
* \(e=4\) would give \(p\mid11\), hence \(p=11\), which has been excluded.

Thus indeed \(e\ge6\).

Set
\[
 n=e-1.
\]
Then \(n\ge5\), \(n<p\), and \(n\) is odd because \(e\) is even. Moreover, using (8),
\[
 P_2=n^2+2n-4=(n+1)^2-5=e^2-5,
\]
which is divisible by \(p\) by (28). All hypotheses (21) are therefore satisfied. The assembly result (22) gives
\[
 a(n)=p.
\]

Together with the direct case \(p=11\), this proves that for every prime \(p\equiv1\) or \(9\pmod {10}\), there exists an index \(n\) for which the reduced denominator of the specified continued fraction is exactly \(p\).
